Here are two facts that changed how I think about small experiments.

The first is how much is on the table. Take 400 pupils and pair them up on
last year's test scores, then flip a coin inside each pair rather than once
across the whole group. The experiment that comes out is as precise as one
run on 1,200 pupils split by a plain coin flip. Nothing was added to the
sample. The only thing that changed was *which* random split came out of the
process.

The second is how easily that is thrown away. A matched experiment analysed
the standard way can be worse than one that was never matched at all. The
precision lives in the pairs, and an ordinary two-sample test cannot see the
pairs, so it reports an interval too wide and misses effects it should have
caught.

<!-- Both figures above are computed in the articles. If the datasets or seeds

       worse off     -> posts/pairwise-matching, "Analysing a matched

There are two methods here, and one measurement they both rest on.
**Pairwise matching** splits the sample into pairs that are as alike as
possible and flips a coin inside each one. **Rerandomization** draws a plain
random split, scores how balanced it came out, and draws again until the
score passes a threshold set in advance. **The Mahalanobis distance** is the
distance metric both of them use to decide how alike two units are, and it is
worth reading when you want to know why correlated covariates are counted
once rather than several times, or what makes the distance fail quietly.

All the code is Python, every figure is reproducible from the source, and the
whole thing lives in
[the repository](https://github.com/AlexanderDBolton/BoostSampleSize).
